item.text: I’m using the dataset-integrity audit workflow to keep the ratings evidence-based, then the social-card workflow to produce a clean generic SVG without exposing session details. I’ll first inspect the data shape and available repository context, then generate and validate both outputs.

--- name: dataset-integrity-audit description: Prepare and audit a scraped or aggregated dataset before any number from it is published. Cross-foots every total against a breakdown that must sum to it, normalises join keys before dedup, separates affected from must-not-change metrics, and catches invented denominators and uncontrolled confounders. Use before publishing statistics, charts, a report page, or social posts built on a data snapshot. --- # Dataset Integrity Audit For the moment between "I have a dataset" and "I published a number from it". Every rule below was paid for by a real defect that reached a real page. None are hypothetical, and none are style preferences. ## The one-line version Count the same thing twice by different routes, and explain the difference to the last record. A residual of one is a defect, not rounding. Internal consistency is not correctness: a single bad rule applied uniformly produces a file that agrees with itself perfectly and is wrong throughout. ## 1. Name the unit before you count Two different, both-correct units are the normal case, not the exception: `(company, person)` pairs are ROLES; distinct persons are PEOPLE. They differ by exactly the serial founders. - Decide which the headline uses, and say so on the page. - Prefer emitting **both** as separate keys. A single count silently changes meaning the day someone redefines it, which makes a monthly series incomparable against its own history without anyone noticing. - Never let one key mean roles in one release and people in the next. Rename instead: `founder_rows` -> `founder_roles` + `founder_people`. ## 2. Normalise every join key before dedup Case, whitespace, trailing slashes, URL vs slug, unicode NFC. Fold before you dedup, not after. The failure this prevents: one LinkedIn slug appeared in the harvest as both `TDaltonC` and `tdaltonc`, same person, same company. Deduping on the raw-case slug counted them as two people, which **fabricated an entity that does not exist** (a 270th serial founder) and, because the second row looked like a second company, recorded that founder's own company as his "other company". One character of casing produced a wrong headline number and a wrong narrative fact. Corollary: a dedup bug does not merely miscount. It invents relationships. ## 3. Cross-foot every total (the highest-value check) For each published total, find a breakdown that must sum to it, and assert it. ``` sum(founders_per_company.values()) == totals.companies_with_founders sum(serial_company_counts.values()) == totals.serial_founders sum(outcomes_by_year[y].n for y) == totals.companies ``` Run `scripts/crossfoot.py` (below) for this. **Know what this check does not catch.** Cross-footing proves a snapshot agrees with itself. It cannot prove the snapshot agrees with reality. On the YC dataset, the corrupt snapshot passed every cross-foot: `founders_per_company` summed to 5,901 and `totals` said 5,901; `serial_company_counts` summed to 270 and `totals` said 270. The whole file was internally consistent and externally wrong, because one bad dedup rule fed every block equally. Cross-footing catches the *other* common defect, where `totals` and the breakdowns are generated by different code paths and drift apart. Both defects are real; this check only finds the second. Rule 3b is what finds the first. **If a total has no breakdown that sums to it, build one.** An unfalsifiable number is not a verified number. Expect some identities to fail legitimately. Year-keyed blocks usually drop records with an unparseable period, so they sum slightly below the grand total. That is fine, and it is exactly the number you must state as the chart's denominator rather than reusing the headline total. Encode the expected shortfall as a `tolerance`, or split the rule, so a real break still stands out. ## 3b. Reconcile two independent counts of the same universe The check that actually found the YC defect, and the one to reach for when a dataset is internally consistent but you do not yet trust it. Count the same universe by two different routes and force yourself to explain the difference **exactly**, to the record: 11,514 harvested rows 11,230 distinct people ------ 284 difference Then account for all 284. 283 were genuine serial founders (256 people at 2 companies, 12 at 3, 1 at 4 = 256 + 24 + 3 = 283). That left **one** unexplained row. Chasing that single row found the case-variant slug, and that one record was what had shifted the coverage count by 73 companies. An unexplained residual of one is not rounding. It is a defect with a small footprint in the count and, usually, a large footprint in the meaning. ## 4. Partition metrics into AFFECTED and MUST-NOT-CHANGE Before regenerating anything, write down which blocks a fix can legitimately move and which it must not touch. Then assert the second set is **byte-identical** after the change. For a founder-side fix: company-only blocks (outcomes by year, industry mix, geography, country counts) must hash identically. If any of them moves, the fix touched the company filter too and something else is wrong. This turns "I think the change was contained" into evidence. It is also the cheapest way to catch a regeneration that silently picked up a different input file. ```bash python3 -c "import json,sys,hashlib d=json.load(open(sys.argv[1])) for k in sys.argv[2:]: print(k, hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(d[k],sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()[:12]) " snapshot.json outcomes_by_year industry_by_year geo_by_year countries ``` ## 5. Regenerate, never hand-patch Fix the engine and re-run it. A hand-edited JSON is correct exactly once and diverges the next time the pipeline runs, with no signal that it has. Then diff key-by-key, old vs new, and account for **every** moved value. A diff you cannot explain line by line is a diff containing a second bug. ## 6. Every published figure must be a key in the snapshot The subtlest failure mode here. Two figures on a slide had been computed ad hoc in a shell one-liner and never stored in the snapshot. When the pipeline was fixed and everything regenerated, those two figures **were not regenerated, because nothing pointed at them**. They survived the correction still wrong, on an already-drafted post, and had to be recomputed by hand. Rule: if a number is going on a page, a slide or a post, it is a key. If you genuinely cannot make it a key today, pin it in code as a named constant with a comment giving its provenance, the date it was computed and the input it was computed against, so the next regeneration has a flagged place to look. ## 7. Denominator honesty Check what fraction of records are missing the field you are dividing by, per period. Coverage that changes over time invents trends. Real example: 46% of the newest cohort carried no industry tag. Dividing by the whole cohort produced a clean, publishable, entirely fictional "AI adoption is collapsing" chart. Dividing by tagged records only, the line does not fall. State the denominator on the artifact itself, not only in a methodology note. ## 8. Control for the obvious confounder before publishing a comparison Any cross-sectional comparison against an outcome is a confounder trap when the population has an age structure. Real example: solo-founded companies died more often than multi-founder ones, a clean story. But older companies die more, and older records list fewer founders. Split into eras and the gap inverts. The naive finding was an artifact of record-keeping, not of founding teams. Before publishing "X correlates with outcome", stratify by time and re-check. If the finding survives, say that it survived: the control is the credibility. ## 9. Sanity floors must name their unit A guard reading `test $COUNT -ge 11514` is worthless when the reader cannot tell whether 11,514 is raw lines, roles or people. Name the unit in the guard message and in the README. A floor whose unit is ambiguous will eventually be compared against the wrong number and either fire constantly or never fire. ## 10. Verify integrity, not row counts Equal row counts prove nothing. Check field-level distributions, null rates, referential integrity, and value ranges before and after. And when checking for orphans, read the `ON DELETE` behaviour first: a `NOT EXISTS` orphan check counts legitimately NULL foreign keys as orphans. ## Pre-publication checklist - [ ] Unit of count named on the artifact; both units emitted where two are valid - [ ] Join keys normalised before dedup - [ ] Every total cross-foots against a breakdown, asserted in code - [ ] Two independent counts of the same universe reconciled to the last record - [ ] AFFECTED / MUST-NOT-CHANGE partition written down, second set hash-identical - [ ] Regenerated from the engine, not patched; every moved value explained - [ ] Every published figure is a snapshot key, or a constant with dated provenance - [ ] Field coverage per period checked; denominator stated on the artifact - [ ] Comparisons stratified by the obvious confounder - [ ] Sanity floors name their unit - [ ] Known limitations disclaimed on the page, in the page's own words ## Scripts `scripts/crossfoot.py` — declare expected identities, get a pass/fail table. ```bash python3 ~/.agents/skills/dataset-integrity-audit/scripts/crossfoot.py snapshot.json rules.json ``` --- name: data-social-cards description: >- Render publication-grade social images (LinkedIn/X/Instagram) for data findings by generating them programmatically from the snapshot JSON, so no figure in an image is ever hand-typed. Covers the data-vs-generated split, sourcing brand tokens from the repo, headless rendering on AX41, the render-bug checklist, and assembling an approval board. Use whenever a chart, statistic, or dataset finding needs to become a social image or a slide - and specifically whenever tempted to ask an image model for a chart. --- # Data Social Cards ## The one rule **An image model never renders the data. Ever.** Image generation cannot produce exact figures, correct axis positions, or a line whose shape matches a series. It produces something that looks like a chart. The entire credibility of a data post is that every figure is verifiable, so a generated chart destroys the thing the post exists to do. The split that works: | Layer | How | Why | |---|---|---| | Numbers, axes, lines, bars, labels | rendered from the snapshot JSON | correct by construction | | Ground texture, atmosphere, illustrative imagery with no information in it | image model | this is what it is genuinely good at | Generated texture underneath rendered type is a real upgrade over a flat fill and costs nothing in accuracy. Use it. Just keep it under the data, never as the data. ## 1. Read the numbers, do not retype them The generator script opens the snapshot and indexes it. Every figure printed on a card, including the ones inside headline and subtitle strings, is an f-string interpolation. ```py S = json.load(open('snapshot-2026-09.json')) IND = {r['year']: r for r in S['industry_by_year']} sub = (f'Consumer companies: {IND[2014]["Consumer"]}% of the 2014 batch, ' f'{IND[2026]["Consumer"]}% of 2026.') ``` If a number appears as a literal anywhere in the script, that is a bug. The point is not convenience, it is that the card and the report page cannot disagree, and next month's refresh re-renders correctly with no edits. The one legitimate exception is a figure computed in the analysis but not stored in the snapshot. Add it to the snapshot rather than typing it in. ## 2. Take the palette from the codebase, not from taste If the piece belongs to a product, open its stylesheet and read the actual token values. Do not eyeball the brand colour from a screenshot and do not invent a palette next to one that already exists. ```bash sed -n '/^:root/,/^}/p' frontend/app/globals.css # light tokens sed -n '/^\.dark/,/^}/p' frontend/app/globals.css # dark tokens ``` Map them to semantic names in the generator so the intent is legible and a rebrand is one edit: ```py INK, PAPER, MUTE = '#0A0A0A', '#FFFFFF', '#A3A3A3' # --rl-bg / --rl-text / --rl-subtle BRAND = '#F94F00' # --rl-accent ALIVE = '#34D399' # --rl-success EXITED = '#F59E0B' # --rl-score-medium ``` **Spend the brand hue on the series the post is about.** A green/amber/red traffic light is semantically tidy and reads as a generic chart with no owner. Putting the brand colour on the one series the headline names, and leaving the rest quiet, makes it the product's chart. Concentrate boldness in one place. ## 3. Format - **LinkedIn portrait 1080 × 1350 (4:5)** is the default: maximum vertical feed space. Square 1080 × 1080 only when the composition genuinely wants it. - PNG for upload (crisp type), max 8MB. A JPEG copy at ~900px is for previews only. - One idea per card. A card that needs a second chart is a second post. Structure that holds up at feed size: mono eyebrow, large display headline with the key phrase in the brand colour, a two-or-three-line mono subtitle carrying the exact figures, the chart, then a rule and a footer with source and URL. The headline is read at thumbnail size; the chart is read after the tap. ## 4. Render headless on AX41, never on the Mac ```bash ssh ax41 'sudo mkdir -p /root/' tar cf - card-*.html | ssh ax41 'sudo tar xf - -C /root/' ssh ax41 'sudo bash -c "cd /root/ && for f in card-*.html; do timeout 90 google-chrome-stable --headless --disable-gpu --no-sandbox --hide-scrollbars \ --window-size=1080,1350 --screenshot=\"\${f%.html}.png\" --virtual-time-budget=8000 \ \"file:///root//\$f\"; done"' ssh ax41 'sudo tar cf - -C /root/ card-a.png card-b.png' | tar xf - ``` Notes that save a debugging round: - `--window-size` must equal the card's CSS pixel size exactly; do not rely on scaling. - `--virtual-time-budget=8000` gives webfonts time to land. Too low and the card renders in the fallback stack, which looks fine in a thumbnail and wrong at full size. - Keep the generated texture as a sibling file referenced relatively. Rendering happens next to it, so there is no need to inline it as a data URI. - If a card comes back blank or half-painted, that is the known headless rAF stall - force `Page.captureScreenshot` over CDP instead of the `--screenshot` flag. - ImageMagick is not reliably present. For downscaling on the Mac use the built-in: `sips -Z 900 -s format jpeg -s formatOptions 78 in.png --out out.jpg` ## 5. Look at every image before showing it Read the rendered PNG. Every card, every re-render. Do not ship a card you have not viewed; the whole point of rendering deterministically is lost if nobody checks the render. These four bugs appeared in a single first pass and all four are invisible in source: | Symptom | Cause | Fix | |---|---|---| | Axis shows `%` with no number | label drawn at `x < 0`, clipped by the viewBox | left padding must exceed the widest label, not the tick | | Two segment labels overlap | per-segment labels under a stacked bar of varying widths | one legend row above; never label narrow segments in place | | Big empty band under the chart | SVG `height` larger than its drawn content, centred by flex | set the viewBox height to the actual content height | | First data point has no tick label | `if year % 2 == 0` skips an odd first year | `if y % 2 == 0 or y in (years[0], years[-1])` | Then check: does the last point's value label match the snapshot, does the axis maximum clip any series, is the headline legible at 25% zoom. ## 6. Generated ground Ask for texture, not content. Enumerate the exclusions explicitly - image models add text and chart-like marks unprompted, and any of those under a real chart is a credibility problem. > Abstract editorial background texture for a data-journalism poster. Neutral charcoal > near-black ground, no green and no blue cast, a faint warm tint upper left only. Faint > hand-drawn ledger grid lines and worn graph-paper rules, uneven ink density, subtle paper > fibre and risograph grain. Soft diagonal light from the upper left. Extremely low contrast, > muted, restrained. Absolutely no text, no letters, no numbers, no charts, no logos, no people. Composite with a scrim so contrast never depends on the generated pixels: ```css background: linear-gradient(160deg, rgba(10,10,10,.55) 0%, rgba(10,10,10,.86) 55%, rgba(10,10,10,.94) 100%), #0A0A0A url('bg-texture.png') center/cover no-repeat; ``` Match the texture's colour cast to the brand ground. A pine-green texture under a neutral near-black palette reads as a mismatch immediately. On AX41, Codex's built-in image generation works through its ChatGPT OAuth session with no API key. `codex exec --sandbox workspace-write --skip-git-repo-check --ignore-rules "Generate one image … and save it to /root//bg-texture.png at 1088x1360"`. Size constraints for gpt-image models: each edge a multiple of 16, ratio ≤ 3:1, total pixels between 655,360 and 8,294,400. The standalone `image_gen.py` fallback needs `OPENAI_API_KEY` and will fail without one; going through `codex exec` does not. ## 7. Approval board Never post directly from the render. Assemble one self-contained HTML page pairing each post's copy with its card, and publish it for review: ```bash cat board.html | openhtmlfeedback --title "…" --project

--agent claude \ --replace-key "::drafts" ``` `--replace-key` updates the same card on re-render instead of piling up. Embed the JPEG previews as base64 data URIs so the page is self-contained. Put on the board, next to each post: the first two lines isolated (all that shows before "see more"), word and character count, and any blocker that must clear before it can go out (a link target that is not live yet, an approval outstanding). The board is where the blockers get seen, so state them, do not assume they are remembered. Nothing is scheduled or posted from this skill. Copy and visuals get approved first. ## See also - `public-dataset-report` - producing the snapshot these cards read from, and killing the findings that should never reach a card. - `linkedin-native-founder-posts` - the copy that goes beside the visual.

Two areas carry explicit friction evidence: visual work has repeated brand/alignment complaints, and research has a prior verification miss; spreadsheet work appears only once, so it must be marked Not measured. I’m treating categories with task breadth but no demonstrated outcome conservatively rather than calling them strong from volume alone.
